title: A generic Result wrapper (cache hits, misses, and faults)
hook: Returning null from Get<T> mixes three different stories: cache miss, stored empty value, and deserialize failure. A small Result<T> or TryGet pattern makes generics practical at API boundaries instead of just textbook List<T> examples.

blocks.text: A Result<T> (or CacheResult<T>, TryResult<T>) is a closed generic type you write to represent outcomes at an input/output boundary. Instead of T? Get(string key) where null could mean miss, empty, or error, you return a struct with explicit states: Hit with a value, Miss with no value, or Fault with an error message. This is where generics become production code — T is closed at the call site (SessionDto, int, TokenClaims) and callers pattern-match on the outcome.

entries.plainDefinition: A type that carries a tag saying which case you are in — hit, miss, or fault — instead of overloading null with many meanings.
A bool-returning method with an out parameter, like Dictionary.TryGetValue.
entries.example: bool TryGet<T>(string key, [MaybeNullWhen(false)] out T value).

entries.plainDefinition: A nullable analysis attribute telling the compiler the out value is unreliable when the method returns false.
entries.example: [MaybeNullWhen(false)] out T value on a cache miss.

blocks.text: Redis GET can miss. A session JSON can deserialize to a DTO with missing claims. An SQS payload can be valid JSON of the wrong shape. If your API is SessionDto? Get(string key), null means all of those at once. Interviewers who have shipped workers want a discriminated outcome. Keep the type small and in your domain — do not pull a fifteen-package Result library to look senior. Use exceptions for programmer errors (null key); use Result for expected I/O outcomes.

blocks.title: When TryGet is enough
blocks.body: Dictionary.TryGetValue is the BCL Result pattern. Mirror it for Redis when you only need hit/miss. Reach for CacheResult<T> when you have a third state — deserialize fault — that you refuse to encode as miss.

items.body: JsonSerializer.Deserialize<SessionDto>. Success with a value is Hit.

items.title: Handle bad JSON
items.body: JsonException becomes Fault with a message — distinct from Miss.

items.title: Caller switches on outcome
items.body: if (result.Hit) use result.Value; else if (result.Error is not null) log fault; else treat as miss.

snippet.label: CacheResult<T> for a Redis session lookup
snippet.explanation: Three factory methods make the three states explicit. Found(T value) takes a non-nullable T so a Hit never stores null. Fault carries the error string separately from Miss.

snippet.label: Using CacheResult at the boundary
snippet.explanation: T is closed as SessionDto at the call site. The caller never wonders whether null means miss or bad JSON. ThrowIfNull on the key handles programmer errors separately.

snippet.label: TryGet alternative for hit/miss only
snippet.explanation: TryGet mirrors Dictionary.TryGetValue. MaybeNullWhen(false) tells nullable analysis the out value is unreliable on false. Add CacheResult<T> when you need Fault as a first-class state.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Returning default! on miss and calling it a hit. Making Result a mutable class with ten properties copied from an exception hierarchy. Using exceptions for Redis misses in a hot high-concurrency path. Using T? on an unconstrained T as a miss signal — it means different things for struct versus class.

interviewTakeaways: A generic Result/TryGet separates miss, hit, and fault at cache and deserialize boundaries.
Unconstrained T? is a poor miss signal; attributes or a wrapper are clearer.
Keep the type small; do not hide ThrowIfNull for broken arguments inside Result.
